items.title: 68533_Sam Jones oral history interview
items.q: The interviewee (Sam Jones) does not speak in the provided context. The mention of Roy Eldridge is made solely by the Interviewer.

ctx.x: See that's the thing that always and the minute we start talking about that, we as black musicians then we suddenly - it's Crow Jim, you know or something like that. We're bad guys that we've got a chip on our shoulder.
Well, maybe we have. You know maybe we've got a chip...Shit if you look at it man, if it weren't for R y Eldridge, where would Gene Krupa be?

items.title: 68533_Sam Jones oral history interview
items.q: So you find another--here's another guy that's playing the trumpet, you know, playing like Roy Eldridge, he joined in.

ctx.x: So, uh, he uh, in those, in those schools, man, you know, they taught you well, you know. They taught you well and they had good teachers in there which they talked--those guys were very technical on the instruments. And, so, each man had a mind of his own, man, you know, and so if a guy come up with an idea we freeze or we go on. And we sit down and think of a melody and make up a--it's all in making up a song it's like you go home and you compose, and you go home and compose a say Larry, that's your--that's…

this man. So now this man is almost like a leader, you see. OK, when he brought that stuff up here to New York, from Kansas City, you see, who knows how long he been doing it down there in Kansas City. The man that taught him. how bad was he? You know? But he's, Charlie Parker swears by the man who taught him, you see. See, he was the greatest man he ever heard, see. The man got to be the uh, uh, uh, a great man, he taught him what he knew, you see. So he came up with this new idea so they brought this stuff up…
